author: zachknows
quote:
GTA VI: A Beautiful World That Forgot What Makes GTA Fun

GTA VI has been a massive disappointment. Rockstar seems more interested in cinematic sequences, superficial features, and forcing players through its story than in delivering the freedom that made Grand Theft Auto great.

Even simple additions feel half-finished. Early on, you can repair part of a house's railing, but not the rest. You can't fix the stairs, and you repair only part of the roof before a cutscene finishes the job. I don't mind home maintenance, but if you're going to introduce it, make it a real mechanic instead of a scripted chore to impress Lucia, someone we barely know.

The story is worse. Lucia pressures Jason into a reckless opportunity involving people neither of them really knows. When he reasonably says no, she walks out and apparently considers that a breakup. Only a later flashback explains she ghosted him. Her childish explanation is simply accepted.

Then she reveals she had his child without telling him. Jason has never met his kid, doesn't know the child's name or face, while Lucia is in prison. Rather than feeling betrayed, furious, or even conflicted, he reacts like it's the happiest moment of his life. It's emotionally absurd.

Lucia's own arrest resulted from another impulsive armed robbery, committed after leaving her child in a nearby store. Yet the story continually expects us to sympathize with her, even as her reckless decisions endanger Jason, get him shot, and send them both on the run. Flawed protagonists can be compelling; protagonists whose choices never receive believable scrutiny are not.

The gameplay repeatedly makes the same mistake: showing us what should have been playable. During a breakfast outing, Lucia spontaneously suggests robbing people at gunpoint. Great! That's exactly the chaotic freedom I want from GTA. Except most of the ensuing string of robberies happens in a cutscene. We barely participate, and after roughly five locations and a police chase, we walk away with about $2,000.

Meanwhile, Moses lets you earn roughly $4,000 in a day from eligible vehicle deliveries alone, before additional missions. Why would a much riskier robbery spree pay so poorly? Even the weapon-shop interface makes it unnecessarily hard to tell which guns you already own, something GTA V communicated better.

When I tried robbing stores freely afterward, Lucia's AI was embarrassing. She stayed outside while I did everything myself. She apparently got into a random shootout, the supposedly alerted police never arrived, and she was just as useless at the next store. For a game centered on criminal partners, you'd expect your partner to actually help commit crimes.

The supposed need to "keep a low profile" is another convenient excuse for restrictions, not a consistent story principle. We're collecting airborne drug drops by boat almost immediately. Another improvised robbery somehow ends with Jason performing a striptease onstage. The script permits absurd risks while restricting the player.

Worst of all, basic sandbox freedom has regressed. Some vehicles cannot even be stolen until you've progressed far enough through the story. In a game called GRAND THEFT AUTO, you must unlock the ability to steal certain automobiles. You can't freely draw your gun in some neighborhoods either. Why is a franchise built around freedom imposing arbitrary limits on its most fundamental activities?

The upgraded police and vehicle systems often compound the frustration. My car gets impounded constantly; reclaiming it can trigger another chase; escaping frequently means tearing through woods and damaging it all over again. Realism should deepen gameplay, not trap players in an exhausting loop of penalties for trying to have fun.

I love realism. The physical weapons, immersive detail, and grounded mechanics are among the few things I appreciate here. But those are largely the strengths Rockstar already demonstrated in Red Dead Redemption 2. All they needed to do was bring that level of immersion into a modern GTA while preserving the crime, nightlife, spontaneous chaos, and freedom of choice that define the series.

Instead, GTA VI offers a gorgeous world full of systems that feel unfinished or unnecessarily restrictive, alongside a story that mistakes forced emotional beats for believable writing. Too often I watch characters commit crimes I should be allowed to commit myself.

I'm sure the game will sell spectacularly after so much hype, but sales aren't proof of quality. If Rockstar interprets that success as approval of this direction, I worry GTA VII won't enjoy the same goodwill.

I didn't wait all these years for an interactive movie that occasionally lets me play. I wanted Grand Theft Auto. For me, GTA VI is a huge step backward. (Had to rate 0 to offset the fake 10/10 reviews.)
